references.text: Jesus responds to the account of the Galileans by warning that everyone must repent, otherwise they will perish in the same way. See [ref:Luk 13:2-5|Luke 13:2-5].
Pilate's role as the Roman governor who had authority over Judea and Galilee. Here in [ref:Luk 23:1-2|Luke 23:1-2] we see Pilate again in a legal context where he is confronted with accusations.

Judas of Galilee is mentioned as a rebel leader. The Galileans were known for revolts against the Romans, which may form the background for Pilate's violent action against the Galileans mentioned in [ref:Apg 5:37|Acts 5:37].

Pilate and Herod's relationship with the Galileans. In [ref:Luk 23:6-12|Luke 23:6-12] Pilate sends Jesus to Herod because he was a Galilean – this shows the political tension surrounding Galilee and Pilate's rule.

Job's friend Bildad claims that God does not reject the innocent and does not hold the wicked in his hand. [ref:Job 8:20|Job 8:20] reflects the traditional view that suffering is always a punishment for sin – the same mindset that the listeners in Luke 13:1 seem to have.

The disciples ask Jesus whether it was the blind man's or his parents' sin that caused the blindness. In [ref:Joh 9:2-3|John 9:2-3] Jesus, as in Luke 13:1-5, rejects the direct link between personal suffering and personal sin.
Pontius Pilate is mentioned as governor of Judea in [ref:Luk 3:1|Luke 3:1], which sets the historical framework for his rule and the events connected to him in the Gospel of Luke.

The Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel that a proverb will no longer be used about fathers eating sour grapes and their children's teeth becoming dull. [ref:Esek 18:1-4|Ezekiel 18:1-4] emphasizes that each person is responsible for their own sin – relevant because the event in Luke 13:1 raises the question of collective guilt.
